report:
## Conclusion

Yes. Denosumab (Prolia) significantly reduces the risk of vertebral fractures in patients with osteoporosis. This is well established by high-quality randomized controlled trial evidence.

The pivotal FREEDOM trial, a large 3-year randomized, placebo-controlled study of over 7,800 postmenopausal women with osteoporosis, found that twice-yearly subcutaneous denosumab reduced new radiographic vertebral fractures by 68% (relative risk reduction) compared with placebo, along with a 40% reduction in hip fractures and a 20% reduction in nonvertebral fractures (NEJM, https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/nejmoa0809493). This effect was consistent regardless of age, baseline bone density, prior fracture history, or previous osteoporosis therapy, and benefits were sustained through 10-year extension data with continued increases in bone mineral density and persistently low fracture rates (FDA label, https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2025/761392Orig1s000lbl.pdf).

However, an important caveat is that discontinuing denosumab is associated with a rapid rebound in bone turnover and loss of bone density, which can increase the risk of vertebral fractures—sometimes multiple fractures—to levels exceeding pretreatment risk. This rebound phenomenon was documented in a post hoc analysis of the FREEDOM trial and its extension (PMC, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5915244/), and has been corroborated in subsequent case series and reviews (PMC, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3617467/).

**Bottom line:** Denosumab is highly effective at reducing vertebral (and other) fracture risk while continuously administered, but abrupt discontinuation without a transition to another antiresorptive agent can paradoxically increase vertebral fracture risk, so treatment cessation should be carefully managed by a physician.
